why: HL-C421. A mock's `requires` row lists the words of the AUDIO PASSAGE and
never the words of the question stem or the answer options, so an item can
pass the book-bounded audit while a candidate cannot read the sentence they
have to choose between. Finding the gap means comparing the paper's stem and
option text against the taught set -- and that comparison is undefined until
somebody writes down which words do not count.
THE LISTS ARE HERE RATHER THAN IN THE CODE because the first three attempts
at this measurement were all computed with a hand-written list that lived in
a script and was never published with the number. HL-C419 records the same
lesson in one line: an aggregate computed with a hand-written list of
categories is only as complete as the list, and the list is invisible in the
result. Derive the categories from the data, write the list down beside the
number, and say what one unit of the count is.
THE UNIT IS A WORD FORM as it appears in a stem or an option, folded to
lower case. Not a lexeme: `alumnos` and `alumno` are one lexeme and two
forms, and the reporter says which form it saw.
functionWordsWhy: Closed-class words: articles, pronouns, prepositions, conjunctions,
determiners, and the handful of high-frequency auxiliaries a candidate meets
as grammar rather than as vocabulary. The corpus teaches these through
grammar lessons whose headwords are not the words themselves, so measuring
them against a HEADWORD set reports every one as missing -- which is the
false positive that produced the rejected 706 figure.
auxiliariesWhy: ser, estar, haber and tener carry the grammar of the sentence far more than
they carry meaning, and the corpus teaches their forms in grammar lessons
(ser vs estar, the perfect, hay) rather than as headwords per form. Listing
the forms is more honest than listing the lemmas, because it is the FORM a
reporter sees on the page and the form is what would otherwise be flagged.
examApparatusWhy: The vocabulary of the instructions rather than of the items: the words a
candidate meets in `Lea el texto y marque la opción correcta`. A real
sitting supplies these in the rubric and they are not what the paper is
testing. `afirmar` is NOT here, and that is deliberate -- it is apparatus in
the two instruction lines but mock 1 item 41 is a SCORED statement whose row
already lists three other words from the same stem, so treating it as
derivationWhy: The rules that decide whether a form is READABLE from something taught.
This is the step that went wrong three times running, every time in the same
direction, so the reporter does NOT use them to drop a word. It uses them to
SORT: a form with a plausible taught relative goes in a bucket that is still
PRINTED, next to the relative it matched, so a reader can reject the match in
THESE ARE SUFFIX RULES, NOT PREFIX RULES, and that is the specific repair.
The hand pass cleared `espacio` by comparing a 3-character PREFIX against the
taught `esperar` -- unrelated words -- and `espacio` vanished until review
found it in the stem of an item that was passing. Stripping declared endings
instead reduces `espacio` to `espaci` and `esperar` to `esper`, so the two
never meet and `espacio` is reported. A test pins that, so adding a prefix
rule later has to break something that says why there isn't one.
minStemLength is 3, and it is deliberately LOOSE. A first draft set it to 4
to cut false matches -- and that silently broke `dice` from the taught
`decir`, whose stem is three letters, pushing a perfectly readable word into
the list a reader has to adjudicate. Because every match is printed beside
the word it matched, a loose rule costs a glance and a tight one costs an
exam item. Loose is the right error to make here.
properNounsWhy: Names of people and places carried by the exam stimulus. They are not
vocabulary and a course is not expected to teach them, but a reporter
cannot tell a name from a noun without being told. Capitalisation is not
enough: a sentence-initial common noun is capitalised too. This list is
read off the papers and must be re-read when a paper changes.
